preoccupation

pree-ahk-yoo-PAY-shuhn -- from Latin prae- ('before') + occupare ('to seize, take possession of'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Preoccupation is a state of being absorbed in thought.

His preoccupation with the weather forecast meant he checked his phone every ten minutes before the wedding.

Example

A student stares blankly at the exam question in front of her, unable to focus, because her preoccupation with that morning's fight with her best friend keeps pulling her mind away.

A preoccupation is exactly that -- one worry seizing all of your attention until you cannot think about anything else.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

absorption: Absorption is the state of being completely engaged in whatever is in front of you, and it is usually chosen and pleasant -- you sink into a good book on purpose. A preoccupation is uninvited: a worry that keeps pulling your attention away from what you should be doing.

fascination: Fascination is intense, delighted interest -- something so appealing that you happily keep watching or reading. A preoccupation grips just as hard but rarely feels good: it is the worry or problem your mind keeps circling back to whether you invite it or not.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indifference: a lack of interest or concern

detachment: emotional distance or lack of involvement

Where it sits · how tightly the mind is gripped

distraction → preoccupation → fixation

distraction vs. preoccupation: A distraction is far milder than a preoccupation -- it tugs your attention away for a moment and is easily shaken off, while a preoccupation keeps dragging your mind back to the same worry all day long.

fixation vs. preoccupation: Fixation is stronger and more extreme than preoccupation -- a fixation is an excessive, hard-to-break focus that borders on unhealthy, while a preoccupation can be temporary and understandable, like worrying before a big test.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -occup-: to seize, take hold of (Latin (occupare))

suffix — -ation: the act or result of; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together: Latin prae- ('before') plus occupare ('to seize') plus the noun suffix -ation: 'the state of being seized beforehand.' A preoccupation grabs hold of your mind before anything else can get its turn.

Use the root in a new word: occupy: The realtor asked whether the upstairs apartment was currently occupied.

Root Check

Word Choice

Preoccupation describes a mental state -- being so absorbed in one worry or interest that other things get ignored. The adjective form is 'preoccupied,' as in 'she seemed preoccupied all evening.'
